title: STOCK, KATHLEEN. Only Imagine. Oxford University Press, 2017, ix + 222 pp., $60 cloth.
abstract: Kathleen Stock's Only Imagine offers an explanatory theory of ‘fictional content,’ of what counts as true within a fiction. Stock takes a bold stand in setting out to defend a view which has historically been, in the author's own words, “very unpopular” (p. 1). The book succeeds in formulating a plausible, lucid, and even fruitful defense of a position which has long deserved closer attention. The core of the view is that an author's intentions, rather than readers’ impressions, the stand‐alone text, or a standard of aesthetic value, are primary in determining what counts as true within the fiction. Stock calls her view extreme intentionalism. More precisely, Stock's central claim is that “an author Au’s utterance x (or set of utterances S) has fictional content that p, if and only if: Au utters x (or S) intending that i) x (or S) should cause F‐imagining that p in her intended readership R; ii) R should recognize this intention; and iii) R’s recognition of this intention should function as part of R’s reason to F‐imagine that p” (p. 15). Let me first give a brief characterization of the main elements of this claim. One thing to note is that Stock is modeling her take on fictional content on a Gricean theory of communication. This accounts for the need that an author intend to have her readers recognize her intention(s). However, Stock takes care to contrast the communication between author and reader and the communication between conversants: the former is generally one‐sided, while the latter may have more than one side. Stock's commitments about what intentions are and which intentions she is concerned with are fairly minimal. She tells us that having an intention entails being committed to bring something about. Stock also adds a constraining condition: an agent can only intend to do something if she does not believe it is impossible. But she allows that intentions “need not be consciously present to an agent” (p. 18), a matter which will be of interest to us later. Finally, Stock clarifies that among candidate intentions she means to pick out, “the intention that animates a given action at the time of acting” (p. 15), in our case, the intention with which the author writes. By “F‐imagining,” Stock means a kind of “propositional imagining,” an imagining with truth‐functional propositional content, which is different from belief in terms of its functional relations to perceptual inputs, other mental states, and behavioral outputs (pp. 20–21), but which need not involve mental imagery, perspective‐taking, or distinctive phenomenology (pp. 23–24). Much more could be said about this notion, which Stock uses to do productive work in the second half of the book. However, I must presently limit myself to a cursory summary. To sum up, Stock's view has it that a text has a certain fictional content just in case its author wrote it animated by the intention that readers, in part by recognizing the author's intention, propositionally imagine the content. Despite the fact that “literary theorists and philosophers alike have poured scorn upon” (p. 1) the idea that authors are the ultimate authorities of their own text (pardon the pun), Stock believes extreme intentionalism is an eminently defensible, wholly misunderstood view. The first three chapters of the book, helpfully peppered with real examples from a variety of literary sources, are dedicated to a direct defense of extreme intentionalism. The later three chapters apply the theory developed in the first half to examine notions of imagination relevant to interpreting fiction, whether truthful testimony can be conveyed through fictional works, the problem of imaginative resistance, and the problem of what fictions are. Although I do not have sufficient room here to explore these constructive applications of Stock's core assumptions, the curious reader will find these chapters accessible and productive. Her novel treatment of imaginative resistance in particular merits serious consideration from specialists. In this review, I briefly describe Stock's general response to the four major challenges she identifies for her view, offer some worries, and then reflect more generally on the extreme intentionalist project. Throughout, for the sake of brevity, I focus on her constructive contributions rather than her criticisms of rival views. A first typical complaint of extreme intentionalism is that it seems to entail “that individual speakers can arbitrarily change or elude” (p. 17) the conventional meanings of sentences. As such, the complaint goes, it rules out “as impossible” that an author might miswrite or misspeak (p. 17). Stock argues that this is a misunderstanding of extreme intentionalism, based on an assumption that the view might involve commitment to individual speaker meaning determining sentence meaning (p. 38). Stock agrees that conventional sentence meanings are not changed by individual speakers’ intentions. She emphasizes that speakers tend to make use of conventional sentence meaning in order to communicate. But Stock cautions, “speaker meaning is not wholly determined” (p. 38) by conventional sentence meaning. For instance, there are cases where conventions are deliberately violated “in order to produce some further non‐conventional implicature” (p. 38). Suppose someone tells the person who has just crashed into their car that they are “clearly a brilliant driver.” The meaning of said utterance is actually the opposite of the meaning of the sentence. But this does not mean an utterance can mean just anything: the utterer cannot intend that it mean something that the hearer could not possibly recognize. So an utterer can fail to communicate a meaning by using the wrong word or sentence or by failing to produce an intended effect in an auditor. Nonetheless, Stock is committed to the primacy of an author's intention. She maintains that “even in cases where in practice the text as it is fails to produce the intended response,” (p. 44) we are to favor speaker meaning over sentence meaning as a determiner of the meaning of the text. This seems like a reasonable commitment for a view like hers to have, and I will not challenge it here. The second major objection to extreme intentionalism worries that it entails that fictional content will be “perniciously hidden” from readers. Stock's entire second chapter is dedicated to responding to this claim. First, she assesses a variety of ways that we might come to understand what is true in a fictional text, such as treating it as conversation, as subject to genre conventions, or as a means of conveying counterfactual information. She concludes that “no strategy of interpretation is applied appropriately without exception to fictional texts” (p. 45). Some texts have hidden meanings, have unreliable narrators, or lack an aim to convey information. Stock does not see the lack of a universal strategy as proof, however, that extreme intentionalism predicts that fictional content is hidden from or inaccessible to readers. In fact, she takes extreme intentionalism to provide a good explanation for the lack of a universal strategy, insofar as it predicts that a given “strategy of interpretation” will typically only be appropriate “when its author (effectively) intends the reader to use it” (p. 45). Because authors differ in their intentions, success of the strategy will be text relative. As a result, interpreters may need to seek out evidence about what an author's wider purposes are in order to then be able to use a correct strategy of interpretation. Stock suggests that a variety of evidence can be used by an interpreter to pinpoint wider authorial purpose, including extra‐textual evidence such as “letters of the author, diaries, interviews, reported conversations …, holograph drafts…, and so on” (p. 79). She is confident that identifying the broader goals of an author will then help readers discern more specific, “nested” authorial intentions in a text. A related challenge to extreme intentionalism objects that it threatens to decentralize the text. Stock calls this worry a “straw man” (p. 85). Extreme intentionalism could not hope to do away with the fictional text because “the text contains or implies all the propositions which the author intends the reader to imagine” (p. 85). I think that there is still a worry here, however. We should of course grant that extra‐textual evidence “is often used by literary critics in interpretation” (p. 79), as Stock points out in her defense against the second objection. My worry is whether critical interest in using extra‐textual evidence is the same one as our interest in sussing out the fictional content of a given text. Extra‐textual evidence may contribute more to seeking what historical insight might be gained from a text or the project of assessing a text's intended literary meaning, literary value or literary associations. Stock emphasizes that these projects are not what she is addressing, except insofar as they have a bearing on content (pp. 2–3). While understandable, this stipulation also seems to unnecessarily divorce fictional texts from their complex interactions with their readership and environment in favor of centering the word and deed of the author and ironically rendering less relevant the author's agency in contributing literary meaning, value, associations, or historical insight. Stock would say that is as it should be: what an author produces and what an author achieves by so producing are not the same thing. At this point it may be productive to ponder a possible objection to extreme intentionalism that Stock does not address. The objection runs as follows. Take the claim that “It is fictionally indeterminate in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (at least, according to its author) what skin colour Hermione has” (p. 1, italics in original). This claim is plausible because the text of the Harry Potter book contains no direct statements about the skin color of its primary female protagonist: the text leaves this indeterminate or ambiguous. However, we might ask whether Rowling's intentions in writing were similarly deliberately ambiguous. In Rowling's own early drawings of her characters, Hermione is portrayed as white. Is this extra‐textual evidence that Rowling only accidentally left ambiguous in the text what skin color Hermione has? There is, of course, other extra‐textual evidence that Rowling presently intends her text to be read ambiguously. The claim required for the objection is only this: there is a possible case, although it may not be the actual case, where Rowling did not initially, while writing, intend to leave Hermione's skin color indeterminate. Suppose we subsequently wanted to take her later intentions to embrace (and, indeed, fix) the indeterminacy in the text. It seems like this opens the door to other post hoc meaning attribution. Why privilege the author's endorsed post hoc meanings over the attributed or found post hoc meanings of other interpreters of the text? Why, indeed, not take the text to be the central determinant of fictional content, rather than the author's intentions? To make the point clearer, distinguish an author's intent at the time of writing that certain fictional truths hold in their writing from the author's disposition to be open to certain fictional truths holding in their writing. It is very clear that Rowling is open to the indeterminacy of Hermione's skin color in Harry Potter. However, it is less clear whether she intended at the time of writing that Hermione's skin color be indeterminate. Under a different theory of fictional content, this is easily settled by the text: the text does not specify Hermione's skin color; therefore it is fictionally indeterminate what skin color she has. If extreme intentionalism is true, however, then we have a difficulty. If Rowling's intentions while writing are authoritative, then Hermione has white skin in the fiction (a dissatisfying result, given that Hermione is portrayed by black‐skinned actresses in the latest Harry Potter stage plays written by Rowling). But if Rowling's later intentions can retroactively revise the fictional content, there seems little reason not to open the door to other determiners of fictional content. While allowing for retroactive intentions to set fictional content does not topple extreme intentionalism, it does give us leverage with which to further destabilize the view, perhaps favoring a milder version of intentionalism in its stead. I suspect that Stock would prefer to say that the earlier intentions settle the matter. If so, we introduce the interesting question of just what sorts of extra‐textual evidence we can be confident in relying on to identify fictional content. The last objection to extreme intentionalism which Stock considers complains that it seems to rule out genuinely unsuccessful intentions to generate fictional content. Stock in fact thinks her account better explains how authors can have genuinely unsuccessful intentions than rival accounts. The problem stems, she thinks, from a misarticulation of the intentionalist view as portraying that fictional content depends on an author's “intention that a fiction mean that p” (p. 82), rather than an author's (reflexive) intention “that readers imagine certain things” (p. 83) as a result of what the author has written. Once we understand this, Stock thinks there are clear cases of unsuccessful intentions: cases where readership recognizes the author's intention but has trouble imagining what they are intended to (p. 83), cases where “the means by which [the author] seeks to achieve her ultimate intention … inadvertently fails” (p. 85), perhaps due to interference from the world, and cases where the reader fails to imagine what the author intends because the author was attempting to imply it rather than state it (p. 86). There are also cases, Stock thinks, where the author fails to provide enough evidence for a reader to imagine what was intended or enough evidence for the reader to recognize what was intended (p. 88). This ends up being “an important tool in aesthetic assessment of fictional texts,” Stock argues, because extreme intentionalism “allows that there can be a mismatch” (p. 92) between fictional content and the effectiveness of the text in conveying it. I find myself agreeing with Stock regarding this explanation for how an author may fail to convey meaning to a reader. However, it seems to me that her requirement that an author intend imaginings in such a specific way (to leave them determinate or purposefully indeterminate or else fail) leaves out an important sense in which authors communicate with readers. Some authors seem to want their texts to acquire meanings, even in the sense of what is true in the fiction, beyond what they themselves could have imbued them with. That is to say, some authors want to invite readers to set meanings not only by under‐specifying a text, but indeed, sometimes by leaving more to engage with than they can contain. I use as my example a selection from Richard Brautigan's Trout Fishing in America (Boston: Houghton Mifflin/Seymour Lawrence, 1967): “Everything smelled of sheep. The dandelions were suddenly more sheep than flower, each petal reflecting wool and the sound of a bell ringing off the yellow. But the thing that smelled the most like sheep, was the sun itself. When the sun went behind a cloud, the smell of sheep decreased, like standing on some old guy's hearing aid, and when the sun came back again, the smell of the sheep was loud, like a clap of thunder inside a cup of coffee” [ibid., p. 50]. It is unclear just which propositions we are being invited to imagine here. Although there is explicit metaphor in this passage, the lines also invite synesthetic readings, mixing sound, visuals, smell, and possibly taste. What would it be for there to be “a clap of thunder inside a cup of coffee”? Are we meant to think of the bitterness feature of coffee when it is said to contain a clap of thunder, or compare its color to the color of storm clouds? The only thing that we can be clear on is that this passage emphasizes that the smell of sheep is incredibly strong. However, if that was all that we were meant to propositionally imagine, why go to all the trouble with the surprising, poetic turns of phrase? I am suggesting that for Brautigan, as for many authors, the text functions like sheet music might: as an invitation to the musician, or in our case the imaginer, to play within the boundaries set by the originator, and make the piece one's own. This may, on occasion, lead a reader's associations to set the actual content of the text, for example, “for me, Brautigan is describing yellow daffodils, whose centers look like bells.” This is perhaps the core of the debate regarding who sets the fictional content of a text. It is not quite so much about whether authors are capable of determining content in their works or whether they are important contributors to what content their works have, but about whether we have, as an audience and as participants, consistent reason to defer to the author's intentions in writing. Kathleen Stock's contention is that extreme intentionalism is the best view because it has the most explanatory value: it does a lot of what we need done when we approach fictional texts as critics and listeners. I believe she has made an excellent case for this point. However, it may also be the case that, when seeking out what the words in a text mean, we are seeking more than an explanation of what makes a text mean what it does. We are seeking justification for its meaning what the author may have intended, as opposed to what we think is an interesting or challenging thing for it to mean. Stock's sturdy reply is that, well, a person wrote the text, and that person had reasons for writing it. Once we realize that, we can do some interesting work.

title: Memory Cut
abstract: The first memory I think I have of my mother, if one can really “have” a memory: We are cutting out pattern pieces from fabric spread out on the dining room table. It was a formal table, used mostly for holiday dinners, when my father would carve up a roasted bird and the rest of us would sit and watch with all the solemnity of an operating theater. But today, on the day that I am remembering, my mother and I are cutting to sew new seams. We are making a dress? A costume? I only remember the big sharp scissors I was forbidden to touch and the little blunt scissors I was allowed to use. Crepey-thin pattern paper, marked with solid and dotted lines that showed you where to cut and where to stitch. Tracing paper embedded with chalk and the spiky tracing wheel that left ghostly lines on the fabric. Many years later, in a different room, I would remember this tracing wheel when someone used a similar instrument on my spine, retracing the memory but reversing the order of pressure, as though the first use of that wheel marked the sensations of a future skin, as though skin could stretch across time.At a certain moment in those afternoons of cutting and stitching, my mother would send me into the next room to read the positions of the big hand and the little hand on the clock. Before the prevalence of digital display, time was still an interplay of embodied speeds, with the big hand tracing the perimeter of the face and the little hand moving more slowly on the inside. We didn't bother with the fugitive movements of the second hand, already escaped to another location even as you tried to mark it. I didn't know how to “tell” time, but I knew how to read the hands on the face and call out the numbers. We talked through the wall. We stopped sewing at the same time every afternoon to do yoga with the lady on television. I was fascinated by the yoga-lady's red leotards, her long braided hair, the patterns she made with her body. A red-clad body in an otherwise empty space. We stretched time by rearranging our bodies, disrupting the habits of household occupation. The little cat with arched back and the fierce lion with outstretched tongue.As my mother loses her memories, I've been trying to recall my first of her, but why privilege the first, as though memory could have an origin? What do I owe her for the memory of the sewing and the yoga—the lines, patterns, tracings, cuts, and stitches? Maybe I only remember these things because they still seem resonant, or maybe I only fabricated them as a “memory,” stitching together things that had nothing to do with one another. She started the clock ticking, but maybe I am the one with the “bad” memory.The clock drawing test (CDT) is one of the tools used to screen people for Alzheimer's. After drawing a circular clock face and adding numbers to mark the hours, the test subject is asked to translate a time—often ten minutes after eleven—into an image. As memory deteriorates, people draw time in increasingly erratic ways. Sometimes there are so many clock hands that they crowd the face and outnumber the hours, dividing time into unfamiliar units. Sometimes the hands extend outside the circle, pointing toward times and spaces not yet mapped. Or the hours are stacked in aggressive piles, while other parts of the face are left empty. Sometimes multiple clock faces and numbers float across the page, new constellations of hours without order. In a support group for Alzheimer's caregivers, a woman tells me that she covers all the mirrors in her house with blankets because her husband no longer recognizes his own face. He is frightened when he sees a stranger looking back at him. As I look at an array of clock test images online, I see one in which the clock face is stretched into a long teardrop shape held perpetually in suspense. Maybe the clock test will go by the wayside as clocks with hands go by the wayside, artifacts of an earlier time. My mother's memory only became “bad” after my father and my brother died in quick succession—two events without an apparent connection. Maybe a rip in the known and trusted fabric of time. Maybe she cannot remember herself without the power of their memories holding her together. Maybe the past is a painful realm, given that they live there.But if memory is painful, she still pursues it, leaving marks on scraps of paper scattered everywhere in her room. Her notes have all the intensity and strangeness of poetry, and I study them with the same kind of attention I give to poems.No mesa? No men at the table? No mensa? No mind? I read this one while sitting at a round table that has traveled from a little Texas farmhouse where my father was born to its current location in a nursing home in Ohio. The table is a space and time traveler. A circular table that has no head, only a cracked leg that causes the surface to sag, making me feel as though space is tilting toward the center of the room. My mother drops letters from the words, remaking objects by remaking their names. She uses her own hand to mark time, crossing out days, activities, and times on the nursing-home events calendar, her lines thick and defiant. Her questions float across the neat grid of days. Where. Where? What. Grace? Is Grace a person or a state of release? She writes I will remember at the bottom of the page, as though there is a will to remember that can be actively invoked, even as her words demonstrate, in circular fashion, that writing can mark the failure of memory.When I visit the nursing home, I enter a temporal society in which the women (mostly women, and the daughters who visit them) meet one another again and again in an uncertain present. Have you met my daughter? Each time, the answer is No, even though I meet these women week after week. My presence is a continual surprise. I can sense them assessing me harshly as the daughter who never visits, perhaps like their own daughters never visit. Bad memories make bad daughters. Each time I leave I gather the week's paper scraps and stuff them in my pockets, carrying my mother's lapses with me. Bible st 3: food at 4 : nothing. Each time I leave I say I'll see you tomorrow, because measures of time longer than tomorrow seem too complex and because I want to convey reassurance in the moment, even though I know my presence will be forgotten as soon as the elevator doors close between us.In the context of the nursing home, more care means smaller rooms, and as she moves into diminishing spaces, the boxes holding her memories take over my own. I lift the lids and the room is full of strangers. The oldest box holds stiff-backed photographs of distant relatives looking suspiciously into the eye of a new technology. As I sift through them, I find a singular image of a woman draped in sheer fabric, arching backward in a dancer's pose. She looks over her shoulder and seems to meet my gaze, her back bending the family tree into shapes I've never considered. A more recent box holds photographs of mothers I hardly recognize, not-yet mothers who were just girls themselves. Girls wearing oversized dungarees cinched at the waist with a belt. Girls leaning on bicycles outfitted with handlebar baskets full of dolls. Another box is full of letters from men whose names I've never heard. Kept for decades, these letters are impossible documents—impossible to read, impossible to discard. One of the envelopes addresses my mother as Bambi, and I imagine a fawnlike figure moving through the letters, leaving tracks between the lines. As I shuffle the letters, I pull the past into the present, replacing parts of my mother with a fawn. She is troubled by these memory boxes full of strangers. She no longer recognizes the faces in the photographs, and sometimes when I visit, I find the photographs face-down on the tables. Boxes closed.During one of my mother's many moves, I stay overnight, trying to help her adjust to the confusion of old objects in new spaces. I put sheets on the bed for her and sheets on the sofa for myself, but she insists that we switch places, because there is a photograph of me on her bedside table. The bed must be mine if my picture is next to it. I try to explain that it is a photograph of me but for her, but her thought follows a storybook logic in which each little bear sleeps in a bed marked with his own picture. I close the discussion by putting the photograph face-down on the table. She falls asleep in bed while I lie awake on the sofa, drinking smuggled red wine and watching an old movie on my laptop with the screen light turned low and headphones over my ears, senses sealed to everything but the flow of digital images and sounds.In the morning, she startles me awake. I know this is a stupid question . . . but are you my daughter? An impossible question. Do I unravel my position as daughter if I say No, or does the question itself already perform this unraveling. In what sense am I a daughter if no one remembers me as daughter. How is the category of daughter preserved if there is no one there to fill it, or if the exhausted person I must appear to be on this particular morning no longer resembles her memory of a daughter. I say Yes, but I don't believe in the power of this word to identify me as anyone other than a stranger who is moving her into smaller and smaller rooms.Still, I find my name written everywhere on her pages, populating the margins alongside anxious notes and questions. Her writing rehearses the meanings and iterations of daughter, assuming a provocatively broken form.When everything goes, will memory somehow jump—across a divide—into me. Her lines end with death, end with daughter, and I follow the repetitions of daughter, My daughter—, daughterΛ, all of us different, all of us going to difference, until the word means nothing. Until the word has to be supplemented with an arrow. All of us at the same time going to daughterΛ, toward the state of an arrow pointing elsewhere—lifting off the map of shining trees.As we walk through a drugstore in a Midwestern strip mall, she asks me repeatedly Is Dad dead? On this particular day, we are waiting on a prescription that, as the doctor said, won't stop memory loss, but might help with adjusting to memory loss. Until there is nothing left to lose but loss itself. We are killing time and walking through aisles of things we no longer need—pet leashes, toys, school supplies—and she is trying to understand my father's death. Has he gone on a trip? Is he coming back? I am drawn to the idea of a trip, but the stakes are too high for anything but a direct answer. He isn't coming back, I say, and she cries as though she is hearing the news for the first time. Dad is dead, I say, and a stranger who overhears me in the hair-dye aisle looks appalled by my terrible sense of timing and apparent lack of emotion. Who would deliver news like this in Rite Aid? I catch the stranger's eye and say loudly, He said you were like a tiger. In one of his last moments he said you were like a tiger. A tiger-woman, not a Bambi-girl. Giving my mother an image of herself as a tiger, or perhaps just giving this image to myself since I know she will forget. We are like tigers with claws to rip into a terrifying present.Tigers wait in slow time, too. And moving toward his death involved forms of time so slow I began to wish for the release of the very event that I was dreading. Wanting to be present-with for a moment of passage but feeling the gradations of loss so attenuated that shared presence seems impossible. Plateaus of uneventful, flat time as nights became mornings buzzing incomprehensibly with life. Aware of the sad irony that a person would spend his final days in a La-Z-Boy recliner, that emblem of suburban leisure and reward, even if it functioned more often as a temporary support for a body exhausted by a lifetime of overwork. A red leather chair that had only ever been his to occupy, perverse taxidermy with the skin turned inside out, a red reminder of something that had once been vibrant but was now cut, stretched, and restuffed. A red-clad body in an otherwise empty space. My mother lost the memory of this scene of death, along with the person she lost. And when she asks me (again), as we are looking for the wedding ring that she has hidden (again), whether the person who gave her the ring is gone, I think about the improvisations she must have had to perform every day, the multiplication of losses and wishes that must continually be experienced anew. It's like everywhere I turn there I am.I try to visit at the same time in the afternoons, as though repetition could produce an impression in time. She always seems to be waiting for someone to arrive, but perhaps everyone is always waiting for someone to arrive. We don't do yoga anymore, but we take long walks together, tracing the same patterns inside the gates of the nursing-home grounds that we have for years. We make a practice of time. We walk in silence that is not uncomfortable, calling upon an archive that feels too deep to be lost. I point out the fall foliage or the spring buds, depending on the season. If it is spring, she questions the chromatic monotony of Ohio. Don't the butterflies here come in different colors? I practice variations on answers I have given dozens of times. At other times, I am caught off guard by a look on her face and her sudden insistence that This Sky is The Most Beautiful Sky I Have Ever Seen in My Life, shocking me into an encounter with beauty unmediated by the comparative shades of memory. When we return to the building, she is always disturbed by a concrete goose that guards the entrance. It must be a Midwestern tradition, but I am unable to explain it. The goose is always dressed in seasonal attire—witch hats and capes in fall, bunny ears and bonnets in spring. I speculate about the kind of person who would spend time sewing clothes for a goose. Each time, she nods in solemn agreement, collaborating with me on memories as cutwork and pattern pieces, points traced into lines and stitched into garments we can wear, at least until they wear out. We don't do yoga anymore, but we still talk through the walls.I am writing this down so I don't forget.

title: Two-Stage TSO-DSO Services Provision Framework for Electric Vehicle Coordination
abstract: High renewable penetration has been witnessed in power systems, resulting in reduced system inertia and increasing requirements for frequency response services. Electric vehicles (EVs), owing to their vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capabilities, can provide cost-effective frequency services for transmission system operators (TSOs). However, EVs that are inherently connected to distribution networks may pose voltage security issues for distribution system operators (DSOs) when supporting TSO frequency. To coordinate both TSO frequency and DSO voltage, this paper proposes a two-stage service provision framework for multi-EVs. At stage one, EVs participate in day-ahead TSO-DSO interactions for frequency reserve schedules; at stage two, EVs make real-time dispatching behaviors in distribution networks for reserve delivery while supporting DSO voltage. Considering the potentially large EV number and environment complexity, a decentralized operation paradigm is introduced for real-time EV dispatches at stage two, while a communication-efficient reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm is proposed to reduce the communication overhead during large-scale multi-agent RL training without compromising policy performance. Case studies are carried out on a 6-bus transmission and 33-bus distribution network as well as a 69-bus distribution network to evaluate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed method in enabling EVs for frequency service and voltage support.

title: Mountain and Cold Weather Warfighting: Critical Capability for the 21st Century
abstract: This monograph posits that military operations in high mountains or intense cold require forces with specialized organization, training, and equipment. The overlap in physical characteristics of mountain and cold weather environments leads to an overlap in the capabilities required of military forces who are able to operate optimally in these regions. The author describes the characteristics of military operations in mountains and cold weather (MCW), and the effects of the MCW environment on each of six warfighting functions. To illustrate the effects of the MCW environment on military operations, the author presents case studies of the cold weather Suomussalmi campaign, which occurred during the Soviet-Finnish Winter War, and the high mountain Kargil campaign, which occurred in the disputed state of Jammu and Kashmir. The latter was one of many bloody confrontations between India and Pakistan. The author also describes those regions that are characterized by high mountains or cold climates that hold strategic importance for the United States. These regions are Central Asia, South Asia, the Caucasus, Iran, the Andes, and the Arctic. The author then catalogs current U.S. military MCW warfighting (MCWW) capabilities, concluding that they are insufficient. Recognizing that the development of a dedicated specialized MCW force is an inefficient and unrealistic goal for the U.S. military, the author recommends a "hedging strategy" to provide a minimally acceptable "off-the-shelf" capability to support U.S. regional combatant commanders. This hedging strategy includes the designation of a Department of Defense executive agent; creation of a high-level programs office to direct and coordinate doctrine, training, and procurement; and the establishment of modern training centers. Finally, the author advocates organizing, training, and equipping specialized units who are designed to provide general purpose forces with MCW-specific expertise and equipment.
